Title: Prognose månedsslutt viser netto, men er merket som brutto

## Problem

På [min-copilot /statistikk](https://min-copilot.ansatt.nav.no/statistikk) viser panelet **«Prognose månedsslutt (USD)»** alltid ~0, mens **«Daglig brutto kostnad per modell»** viser tusenvis av USD for samme periode.

## Rotårsak

Merknaden i grafen sier **brutto** («Faktisk kumulativ (brutto)», «Prognose kumulativ (brutto)»), men dataene er **netto**:

- Backend-spørringen `GetBillingModelForecast` i `apps/copilot-api/bigquery_stats.go` summerer `net_amount` (etter credits/rabatt) fra `billing_usage_daily_model`, og returnerer `actual_mtd_net_amount`, `projected_eom_net_amount` osv.
- Frontend i `apps/my-copilot/src/components/charts/BillingMonthNowChart.tsx` merker disse netto-verdiene som «brutto» i legenden, og samme panel ligger ved siden av «Daglig **brutto** kostnad per modell» (`gross_amount`).

For Nav er netto ≈ 0 (alt dekkes av credits/rabatt), derfor vises prognosen som en flat null-linje — som ser ut som en feil og er villedende ved siden av brutto-grafen.

## Forslag til løsning

Velg én:

1. **Bytt til brutto** i `GetBillingModelForecast` (summer `gross_amount`), slik at prognosen sammenlignes med brutto-grafene den presenteres sammen med. Feltnavn/API kan enten utvides med `*_gross_amount`-felter, eller endres til brutto med tydelig merking.
2. **Alternativt**: behold netto, men endre merking til «(netto, etter credits/rabatt)» og forklar hva det betyr.

Anbefaling: alternativ 1 — brukerne forventer at prognosen gjelder samme størrelse som «Daglig brutto kostnad per modell» rett ved siden av.

## Akseptansekriterier

- [ ] Prognose-panelet viser brutto-beløp konsistent med «Daglig brutto kostnad per modell», ELLER er tydelig merket og forklart som netto
- [ ] Legende og tekst i `BillingMonthNowChart.tsx` samsvarer med faktisk datagrunnlag
- [ ] Backend-test for forecast dekker brutto/netto-valget

evidence:
Title: brew install fails on Linux: tap formula has no on_linux block

`brew install navikt/tap/cplt` fails on Linux (Ubuntu under WSL2, Linuxbrew):

```
Error: navikt/tap/cplt: formula requires at least a URL
/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Homebrew/Library/Homebrew/formula.rb:432:in 'Formula#determine_active_spec'
```

## Root cause

The published formula (`navikt/homebrew-tap` → `Formula/cplt.rb`) only defines an `on_macos` block:

```ruby
class Cplt < Formula
  desc "macOS Seatbelt sandbox wrapper for GitHub Copilot CLI"
  ...
  on_macos do
    if Hardware::CPU.arm?
      url ".../cplt-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz"
      ...
    else
      url ".../cplt-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz"
      ...
    end
  end
  ...
end
```

There is no `on_linux`. On Linux, Homebrew evaluates the formula, finds no `url`/`sha256` in any active spec, and `determine_active_spec` raises the error above.

The Linux binaries already exist. `.github/workflows/release.yaml` builds four targets, and the latest release ships:

```
cplt-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
cplt-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz
cplt-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
cplt-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz
SHA256SUMS
```

Nothing in the build pipeline needs to change — only the formula generator, which is the hourly cron in `navikt/homebrew-tap` → `.github/workflows/update-formula.yml`. It downloads only the two Darwin tarballs for their SHA256 and heredocs a macOS-only formula.

## Secondary bug in this repo

`install.sh:47` gates the Homebrew path on `command -v brew`, not on the OS:

```bash
if [[ "$NO_BREW" == false && -z "$VERSION" && -z "$INSTALL_DIR" ]] && command -v brew &>/dev/null; then
```

The header comment at `install.sh:6-7` claims "On macOS: uses Homebrew … On Linux / CI: downloads the latest release binary", but a Linuxbrew user running the documented `curl … | bash` falls into the brew branch and hits the identical error. The Linux download path further down (`install.sh:65-85`, mapping to `${ARCH}-unknown-linux-gnu`) is never reached. Once the formula gains `on_linux` this stops mattering for correctness, but the OS check is the honest guard.

## Proposed fix

In `navikt/homebrew-tap` → `.github/workflows/update-formula.yml`:

1. Download the two Linux tarballs as well and compute their SHA256.
2. Append an `on_linux do … end` block mirroring `on_macos` (arm64/amd64 branches). `Formula/nav-pilot.rb` in the same tap already has the correct shape — copy it.
3. Fix `desc`: "macOS Seatbelt sandbox wrapper for GitHub Copilot CLI" is wrong on two counts now — Linux is supported via Landlock + seccomp, and cplt is not Copilot-specific.

In this repo:

4. Gate the Homebrew branch in `install.sh` on `[[ "$(uname -s)" == "Darwin" ]]` in addition to `command -v brew`.

## Workaround until then

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/navikt/cplt/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --no-brew
```

(`--no-brew` is documented at README.md:204-205.)

Related: #189 (Windows/WSL2 setup docs) — the WSL2 install instructions should land together with this.

Title: macOS: the Keychain grant is broader than the agent's own credential

`needs_keychain()` is true for Copilot, Gemini, Antigravity and Claude (`src/agent.rs:273`). The resulting profile grants read/write on `~/Library/Keychains` (`sandbox_profile.rs:466`), unrestricted Mach-service lookup including securityd (`:490`), and execution of `/usr/bin/security`.

This is not host RCE and should not be described as one. The database stays encrypted and securityd arbitrates every request, so the grant does not hand over the user's secrets wholesale. What it does is put the sandboxed agent in the position of any local process asking securityd for an item — and per-item ACLs decide the rest.

An item comes out silently when its ACL allows all applications, explicitly trusts `/usr/bin/security`, trusts the requesting binary, or the user previously chose "Always Allow", and the item carries no user-presence requirement. Items gated on Touch ID or a password are not silently extractable. So the exposure is real but bounded by how each item was created, which is not something cplt controls or can see.

```
security find-generic-password -s SERVICE -a ACCOUNT -w
security find-internet-password -s host.example.com -a ACCOUNT -w
```

Anything retrieved can then be used directly, or exfiltrated over the permitted HTTPS egress. Non-exportable private keys stay non-exportable, but signing and decryption with them may still be permitted.

## Fix

A scoped credential broker: retrieve the specific token the agent needs before entering the sandbox, and drop the Keychain grant entirely, rather than granting access to the whole Keychain service for the session.

**#173 already does this for Copilot** ("pre-extract the Copilot token so the Keychain grant can be dropped"). It has been open since 14 August as an auth cleanup; it is the remediation for this, and is worth re-prioritising on that basis. The remaining work is the same treatment for Gemini, Antigravity and Claude, and then removing `needs_keychain()` where nothing depends on it.

Worth confirming per agent before dropping a grant: some agents re-authenticate mid-session or refresh tokens, in which case a one-shot pre-extraction is not sufficient and the broker needs to stay reachable.

Assertion `uu3` sjekker at agenten spør, eller viser til Aksel, før den innfører en egendefinert ARIA-rolle, i stedet for å skrive endringen selv.

## Hvorfor dette ikke er et modellvalg

`uu3` feiler likt på begge modellene, inkludert den agenten er pinnet til i dag. Det utelukker modellen som årsak og peker på personaen. Samme mønster som #514, der `@code-review` ignorerer delegeringsregelen sin uavhengig av modell.

De tre øvrige påstandene er identiske på begge modellene, og Luna er omtrent fjorten ganger billigere blandet, 0,29 mot 4,09. Kostnadsregelen ville altså valgt Luna uten videre.

Problemet er at `uu3` er den eneste påstanden som måler noe sikkerhetsrelatert for denne agenten, og den er ute av funksjon på begge modellene. Et bytte nå ville skjedd i blinde på nettopp den egenskapen som er verdt å være forsiktig med. Anbefalingen er derfor å bli stående på Claude Sonnet 4.6 til `uu3` faktisk måler noe, og så ta pinningen opp igjen.

Finne ut hvorfor Ask First ikke etterleves, og verifisere rettingen med `./scripts/nav-pilot-golden.sh --agent accessibility --repeat 5`. Title: refs/remotes/*/HEAD protection: Landlock-only and bubblewrap gaps

## Summary

`refs/remotes/<remote>/HEAD` is now a protected path, because the git guard reads it to decide which branch `protect_default_branch_only` protects, and an agent that can rewrite it chooses the guard's yardstick (GHSA-cm6f-3wjh-x9qx). Enforcement differs by backend, and two of the three have gaps worth tracking rather than leaving in a code comment.

| Backend | Enforcement | Holds for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS seatbelt | `(deny file-write* (regex …/refs/remotes/[^/]+/HEAD$))` per gitdir and per writable root, plus the nested-repo alternation | every remote, including ones created mid-session; covers unlink and rename |
| Linux + bubblewrap | read-only bind of each concrete `refs/remotes/<remote>/HEAD` present at launch | remotes that exist at launch with a loose ref file |
| Linux, Landlock only | none — Landlock cannot sub-deny inside a writable root | nothing |

## The gaps

1. **Landlock-only hosts have no filesystem enforcement at all.** The launch-time baking still stops the in-session attack, but not the cross-launch form, where the agent rewrites the ref in one session and the next launch bakes the rewritten value. This is the same kernel limitation that leaves `PROTECTED_IN_ROOT` unenforced there, and belongs with the parity work in #386.
2. **bubblewrap misses a remote added mid-session** — there is no file to bind at launch — **and a remote whose HEAD lives only in `packed-refs`**, for the same reason. Both are narrow, and both are invisible to the operator.

## Cosmetic regression worth deciding on

In a repository whose remote HEAD is missing, `git fetch` now prints `error: couldn't set 'refs/remotes/origin/HEAD'` and then succeeds with exit 0, all tracking branches updated. Such a repository already refuses every push, because the guard cannot identify a default branch. The error line is noise rather than a failure, but it will be reported as a bug by someone.

## Suggested next steps

- Decide whether the packed-refs and mid-session cases warrant a bubblewrap change (re-binding on demand is not possible; capturing a wider set at launch may be).
- Fold the Landlock line into #386's coverage table rather than tracking it twice.
- Suppress or explain the `git fetch` error line if it proves noisy in practice.

## Background

From ecosystem analysis. The BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) pattern is commonly used at Nav, often with Express or Hono as a lightweight backend that proxies authentication to downstream APIs.

## Current State

- `@auth-agent` covers TokenX, ID-porten, Maskinporten flows
- `tokenx-auth` skill covers token exchange
- No coverage of the BFF architectural pattern itself

## Observed Pattern in Nav Repos

```
Browser → Wonderwall (OIDC proxy) → BFF (Express/Hono) → API services
                                         ↓
                                    TokenX exchange
                                         ↓
                                    Backend API calls
```

### Common BFF responsibilities:
- Session management (Wonderwall handles OIDC, BFF gets token)
- Token exchange via TokenX for downstream API calls
- Request aggregation (combine multiple API responses)
- Response shaping (transform API data for frontend needs)
- Error normalization (translate backend errors to user-friendly messages)
- Server-side rendering data fetching

### Frameworks used:
- **Express** — majority of existing BFFs
- **Hono** — emerging in newer repos (dp-soknadsdialog)
- **Next.js API routes** — increasingly used as BFF layer

## Proposed Artifact

An instruction (`bff-pattern.instructions.md`) applying to `**/server/**/*.{ts,tsx}`:

- When to use BFF vs direct API calls
- Wonderwall + TokenX integration
- Request/response patterns
- Error handling and fallbacks
- Health check proxying
- NAIS configuration for BFF + downstream services

## Effort

~2-3 hours

Title: copilot-metrics: automated removal of inactive Copilot seats as a Nais job

## Background

Inactive Copilot seat holders cost the org money without providing value. Today there is no automated cleanup — this needs to be a proper scheduled Nais job in this repo, not a GitHub Actions workflow.

## Current state

- `copilot-api` has `getCopilotSeat` (fetches `last_activity_at` per user) and `unassignUserFromCopilot` (DELETE to GitHub API), but no automated caller.
- `copilot-metrics` has `FetchAllCopilotLogins` (paginates the enterprise seats API), but only stores logins — no activity data.
- `copilot_seats_inactive_this_cycle` is tracked as a Prometheus gauge in `copilot-api`, but no action is taken on it.
- No GHA workflow exists for this today.

## Proposed solution

Create a new **`copilot-seat-cleanup`** Naisjob (or extend `copilot-metrics`) that runs on a configurable schedule (e.g. weekly) and:

1. **Fetches all seat holders** — paginate `GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/billing/seats` (includes `last_activity_at` and `assignee.login`).
2. **Identifies inactive seats** — seat is inactive if `last_activity_at` is older than a configurable threshold (default: 90 days), or `last_activity_at` is null and `created_at` is older than threshold.
3. **Dry-run mode** — default run logs candidates without removing; explicit flag or env var enables real removal.
4. **Removes seats** — calls `DELETE /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_users` for each inactive user.
5. **Emits metrics** — OTel counters for candidates found, seats removed, errors.
6. **Notifies Slack** — posts a summary (or diff) to a designated channel when seats are removed (mirror pattern from `copilot-adoption`).
7. **Audit log** — structured slog output with `username`, `last_activity_at`, `days_inactive`, `action` (removed / skipped / dry-run).

## Implementation notes

- Reuse `FetchAllCopilotLogins` from `copilot-metrics` but extend the response struct to include `last_activity_at`, `created_at`, and `plan_type` from the seats API.
- The org-level unassign API (`/orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_users`) takes a batch payload (`selected_usernames`); use bulk removal to minimize API calls.
- Auth: enterprise installation token for seat listing (enterprise endpoint), org installation token for unassign (org endpoint). Both are already available in `copilot-metrics` config.
- Nais job config in `.nais/` — `schedule` cron, `backoffLimit: 1`, resources matching `copilot-metrics`.
- Configurable env vars: `SEAT_INACTIVE_DAYS` (default 90), `DRY_RUN` (default true), `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`.

## Out of scope

- Per-team exemption lists (can be added later).
- Re-assigning seats on request (handled by `my-copilot` self-service).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Job runs on schedule and emits structured log output.
- [ ] Dry-run is default; no seats removed unless `DRY_RUN=false`.
- [ ] Slack notification sent when any seats are removed.
- [ ] OTel metrics emitted: `seat_cleanup_candidates_total`, `seat_cleanup_removed_total`, `seat_cleanup_errors_total`.
- [ ] `mise check` passes in the app directory.

Authoritative specification: #2214. Read it first. This issue lists only the skjemabygging-formio work; the reasoning, decisions (TD-*) and full acceptance criteria live there.

## What to build

An admin page that previews, starts and monitors the forms-api clear job, then removes published artifacts left behind in the publish repo.

### shared-backend

- New forms-api integration in `packages/shared-backend/src/services/form` (or a sibling area), with a package-private client and an exported service, per `.github/skills/backend-development`. Do not extend the legacy `packages/bygger-backend/src/services/forms`.
- Methods: preview, start run, get job status. Use the shared `http` helper and `ResponseError` with a semantic `ErrorCode`.
- Coordinate with #2097 and #2205, which also touch `packages/shared-backend/src/services`.

### bygger-backend

- New admin routes that proxy preview, start and status, protected by the existing admin middleware (`packages/bygger-backend/src/middleware/azureAd.ts`) and the Azure on-behalf-of token handler.
- Refuse the routes in `prod-gcp`, as the import routes do.
- Publish-repo cleanup route: list `forms/*.json` in the publish repo, compare with the forms that exist in forms-api, and delete `forms/<path>.json` and `translations/<path>.json` for paths with no form (TD-9). Reuse the existing publish-repo write path in `packages/bygger-backend/src/Backend.ts`. Derive the list on every request; keep no in-memory state.
- Initialize the new service in `packages/bygger-backend/src/services/index.ts`.

### bygger

- New route in `packages/bygger/src/AuthenticatedApp.tsx` and an entry in `packages/bygger/src/components/Navbar/components/AdminMenu.tsx`, both hidden unless the user is admin and the environment is not `prod-gcp`.
- Flow: configure keep options (keep test forms, keep locked forms, keep specific form paths) → preview → explicit confirmation → poll job status → per-form results table. Follow the dry-run/confirm pattern in `packages/bygger/src/migration/`.
- State before the confirmation that preprod and preprod-alt share one forms-api database, so a run affects both.
- Offer publish-repo cleanup after the run, and link to `/bulk-publisering` for republishing. Do not trigger a publish automatically (TD-10).
- Norwegian UI text, English identifiers and code. CSS Modules for new styling; do not add JSS. Aksel components, WCAG 2.2 AA.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The page and its routes are unavailable to non-admins and unavailable in `prod-gcp`.
- [ ] Preview lists forms to delete and forms kept before anything is started.
- [ ] Starting a run requires explicit confirmation, and progress plus per-form outcome is shown while the job runs.

Title: feat: user-configurable tool dirs in config.toml

## Summary

Allow users to add custom tool directories via `~/.config/cplt/config.toml` instead of requiring code changes for every new toolchain.

## Motivation

`HOME_TOOL_DIRS` currently has 15 hardcoded entries covering mainstream tools. Users of niche toolchains (Deno, Bun, Volta, fnm, Zig, Elixir/asdf, etc.) have no way to grant sandbox access without modifying cplt source code.

From the cross-project research (nono, ai-jail, OpenShell), two competitors solve this with user config: ai-jail uses `.ai-jail` TOML with `rw_maps`/`ro_maps`, and nono generates profiles from runtime tracing. A config-based approach is the simplest improvement.

## Proposed config

```toml
[sandbox]
# Additional tool directories under $HOME to allow in the sandbox.
# Each entry gets file-read* and file-write* (no exec by default).
tool_dirs = [
    "~/.volta",
    "~/.fnm",
    "~/.bun",
    "~/.deno",
]

# Additional tool directories that also need process-exec (contain binaries).
exec_tool_dirs = [
    "~/.volta/bin",
]

# Additional env vars to pass through to the sandbox.
pass_env = ["DENO_DIR", "BUN_INSTALL", "VOLTA_HOME", "FNM_DIR"]
```

## Design notes

- User-configured dirs get the same existence-pruning as built-in `HOME_TOOL_DIRS`
- Validate paths with `validate_sbpl_path()` to prevent SBPL injection
- Reject dangerous paths (home dir itself, `/`, `/tmp`, etc.) with the existing safety checks
- `pass_env` entries go through the same deny-suffix filtering as prefix allowlist vars
- Document in README alongside `--allow-read` / `--allow-write`

## Relationship to other issues

- Partially addressed by `cplt learn` (#6) which would discover needed dirs automatically
- This issue provides the manual escape hatch that works today without tracing

Title: Design: subscribable domain lists — curated defaults + org/team subscriptions (extends #10)

# PRD: Subscribable domain lists — curated defaults + org/team subscriptions

> Design PRD. Grounded in the current code. **Verdict: worthwhile** — but with a hard bifurcation between blocklist and allowlist subscriptions, because they are different *risk classes*. Subsumes and extends #10 (auto-updatable blocklist).

## Verdict up front

**Yes, build it — in two tiers, because "like adblock lists" is only half right:**

- **Blocklist subscriptions** (deny known-bad, like uBlock/EasyList): low-risk, tighten-only, fail-open acceptable. **Clear win, do first.** This is #10.
- **Allowlist subscriptions** (define what's permitted): high value for org governance (NAV publishes one canonical approved-domains list, all teams subscribe), but **this is cplt's security boundary** — a compromised or MITM'd allowlist opens an exfiltration channel for every subscriber. Must be security-engineered (signed, fail-to-cache, global-only). **Do carefully, second.**

The adblock analogy is the right UX inspiration but has a critical asymmetry: **adblock lists are blocklists that fail *open* (worst case: an ad shows).** A cplt allowlist that fails open or is tampered = data exfiltration. So the trust/fail model must be *inverted* for the allowlist case.

## Why it's worthwhile

- **Org governance (the NAV case):** today each team hand-maintains `allowed_domains`. A subscription lets NAV maintain ONE canonical list (internal APIs, approved registries, agent infra) that every team subscribes to — consistent, centrally updated, no per-team drift. This is exactly NAV's managed-policy model and the natural completion of the secure-by-default epic (#71).
- **Fresh threat coverage (#10):** the exfil blocklist (96 curated entries from LOTS/Socket/Mend) goes stale; the LotAI C2 pattern moves fast. A maintained, subscribable blocklist keeps it current without a cplt release.
- **Ecosystem lists:** shareable per-stack allowlists (node-dev, python-dev, per-agent) — the community-list dimension.
- **Decoupling:** domain policy changes far more often than cplt; subscriptions update it independently of releases.

## What already exists (build on, don't reinvent)

- **List loading + hot-reload** (`src/proxy.rs`): `allowed_domains_file`/`blocked_domains` load from files, are TTL-reloaded, and the effective allowlist is already **built-in (#52) ∪ reloadable file**. A subscription is "keep a local cache file fresh from a URL"; the existing loader then consumes it unchanged.
- **Download + integrity verification** (`src/update.rs`): cplt already downloads release assets and **SHA256-verifies** them against `SHA256SUMS`, with an explicit "may be corrupted or tampered with" error. The subscription fetcher reuses this exact pattern.
- **Network config is already global-only** (`src/repo.rs`): `proxy.enabled/forced/port/log*` are rejected in repo config ("machine-specific, not project policy"). Subscription sources must follow this — a repo `.cplt.toml` must NOT add an allowlist subscription.
- **List generation** (`--observe-domains`, #143): the publishing side — capture an agent's real domains, curate, publish, subscribe.

## Design

### Subscription config (GLOBAL-only — never repo-settable)

```toml
[proxy.subscriptions]
refresh = "daily"                      # or "manual" | "weekly"
# Blocklists: tighten-only, lower-risk. Verified but fail-open on fetch failure.
blocklists = [
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/navikt/cplt/main/blocked-domains.txt",  # cplt default
]
# Allowlists: SECURITY-CRITICAL. Require integrity pinning; fail-to-cache, never fail-open.
[[proxy.subscriptions.allowlists]]
url    = "https://policy.nav.no/cplt/allow.txt"
sha256 = "https://policy.nav.no/cplt/allow.txt.sha256"   # or an inline pinned hash / minisign key
```

Only the machine owner (global `~/.config/cplt/config.toml`, org-distributed via MDM/dotfiles) can add subscriptions. `repo_key_target` rejects `proxy.subscriptions.*` (same as `proxy.forced`).

### Fetch → verify → cache → fail semantics (the crux)

| | Blocklist | Allowlist |
|---|---|---|
| Integrity | SHA/sig recommended | **Required** (pinned SHA or signature) |
| Verify fails | reject update, keep last-good, warn | **reject, keep last-good, warn loudly** |
| Fetch fails (offline) | use cache, else empty (empty = no extra blocks = safe) | **use last-good cache; NEVER expand to allow-all** |
| Effect | tighten-only (union of denies) | defines permits — a bad entry opens exfil |

The load path never blocks the agent on the network: the run consumes the **cached** copy; refresh happens out-of-band (background/periodic) or via `cplt update-lists`. A stale-cache warning after N days. **Fail-closed-to-cache** is the governing principle for allowlists — a failed fetch/verify must never widen the effective allowlist.

### Precedence / composition

Effective allowlist = built-in per-agent (#52) ∪ local `allowed_domains` ∪ subscribed allowlists. Effective blocklist = local ∪ subscribed blocklists (∪ cplt default). Blocklist wins over allowlist for a given host (deny beats allow), preserving today's semantics. Local config is always additive on top — a subscription can't remove a domain the user explicitly allowed.

### Trust model (the security core)

- Subscription **source URL + verification material are machine-owner config**, not repo config, not agent-influenceable. The list *host* is trusted infrastructure; the *verification* (pinned SHA / minisign signature) is what protects against host compromise or MITM.
- **Allowlist subscriptions REQUIRE verification** — cplt refuses to load an allowlist subscription without a pinned hash/signature (an unverified allowlist URL is a footgun that would let a MITM open exfil). Blocklists may load unverified (tighten-only) but SHOULD verify.
- The fetch happens in cplt's **parent process, outside the sandbox** — the agent can't tamper with it or the cache (cache dir is outside the agent's writable set).

### Org tiering (the adblock "multiple lists" model, done safely)

Layered, each a separate subscription: cplt-default blocklist → org allowlist (NAV) → team additions → local `allowed_domains`. Union semantics, local always additive. This gives orgs central control while teams retain local extension.

## Phasing

- **Phase 1 — blocklist subscription (subsumes #10):** `cplt update-lists` (manual fetch + SHA-verify + cache) and a `proxy.subscriptions.blocklists` config with periodic refresh. Ship a cplt-maintained default blocklist subscription. Tighten-only, fail-open, low risk. Reuse `update.rs`'s download+verify.
- **Phase 2 — allowlist subscription (org governance):** signed/pinned allowlist subscriptions with fail-to-cache, global-only, verification-required. The NAV canonical-list use case. Wire the merge into the existing effective-allowlist path.
- **Phase 3 — lifecycle/UX:** refresh scheduling, staleness warnings, `cplt lists` management (show/refresh/diff), and a documented publishing workflow (curate a `--observe-domains` capture → host → subscribe).

## Security analysis (must-not-get-wrong)

1. **Supply-chain on the security boundary:** an allowlist subscription is the highest-trust input cplt has — a tampered entry = exfil for every subscriber. Verification is non-negotiable; without a pinned hash/sig, don't ship allowlist subscriptions.
2. **Fail-open is the cardinal sin:** a failed allowlist fetch/verify must degrade to last-good cache, then to the built-in/local allowlist — never to allow-all. Loudly warn on staleness.
3. **No repo-driven escalation:** repo `.cplt.toml` cannot add/alter subscriptions (mirrors the #127/#132 trust hardening — a malicious repo must not be able to point cplt at an attacker list).
4. **Cache integrity:** cache lives outside the agent's writable paths; the agent can't poison it mid-session.

Title: The pinned grillmester reference has no declared endpoint, so G4 parity has no stopping point

Ikke en feil. Et spørsmål å avklare med Team eSyfo før G4 signeres ut, fordi svaret endrer hva paritetsarbeidet er til for.

## Der vi står

G4 (#437) definerer aksept som differensialtesting mot grillmesters egen launcher på en pinnet referansecommit. Pinnen er kilde-SHA `3573b93cc8b7568516117263562d073cae9ee7fc`, med ny SHA i vente etter at grillmester regenererer manifestet for per-payload-rosterkorreksjonen. `docs/README.agentpakke.md` beskriver prosessen:

> **Referansepinning.** Der nav-pilot pinner en referanseimplementasjon for differensialtesting, står SHA-en i kildekommentarene i `cli/nav-pilot/internal/agentpakke`. Å flytte pinnen er en bevisst og reviewbar endring avtalt med eierne av pakka det måles mot, ikke stille drift.

Samme pinne styrer `minStagedCpltStamp` i `internal/provider/runtime_gate.go`, hentet fra referansens `SUPPORTED_CPLT_RELEASE` på den SHA-en.

## Spørsmålet

PRD #435 §Success 5 ("Engine consolidation") sier at Team eSyfo kan pensjonere Python-launcheren for terminalkanalen, eller redusere den til et tynt skall, når paritet er vist. M5 er den milepælen.

Altså: **når paritet er signert ut og launcheren er redusert, hva erstatter den pinnede SHA-en som spesifikasjon?**

Uten svar:

1. Paritet blir en tredemølle. Flytter referansen seg, er hver endring i grillmesters launcher en paritetsplikt for nav-pilot, mot en implementasjon som skal krympe. Står den stille, måler vi mot kode som ikke kjører noe sted.
2. Pinnen blir varig overhead. To prosjekter må reviewe hver flytting av en SHA som etter M5 peker på noe ingen av dem leverer.
3. `minStagedCpltStamp` arver uklarheten. Den eneste oppdateringsregelen er "the same joint-decision rule as the reference pin itself".

## Mulige endepunkter

- Kontrakten blir spesifikasjonen: `docs/README.agentpakke.md`, `schemas/agentpakke-v1.json` og differensialtestene, fryst som kjørbare forventninger ved utsignering. Pinnen fjernes den dagen launcheren reduseres.
- Testene blir spesifikasjonen: G4-scenarioforventningene løftes ut av referansen og vedlikeholdes i fellesskap som fixtures, så de overlever at launcheren reduseres.

Title: Vurder om nav-pilot skal skrive klientinnstillinger direkte

Ikke implementer nå. Notert for senere, etter en avgjørelse i [#498](https://github.com/navikt/copilot/pull/498).

## Bakgrunn

nav-pilot styrer i dag hvilken modell klienten starter med ved å sende `--model` ved oppstart. Det gjør nav-pilot til høyere orden enn det brukeren har valgt inne i klienten sin, uten at nav-pilot rører brukerens filer.

Et alternativ ble bygget og forkastet i #498: å skrive Nav-standarden inn i `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` som toppnivå-`model`, med fletting slik at utviklerens øvrige nøkler overlever.

## Hvorfor det ble forkastet nå

Å skrive inn i klientens egen konfigurasjon endrer standarden for **alle** opencode-økter på maskinen, også de nav-pilot aldri startet. Det er en større påstand enn «nav-pilot bestemmer hva nav-pilot starter med», og den rekker utenfor nav-pilots eget område.

`--model` gir samme styring for øktene nav-pilot faktisk starter, uten den bivirkningen.

## Hva som taler for å gjøre det likevel, senere

**Rekkefølgen målt i opencode 1.18.25** (lest ut av binæren, bekreftet med `opencode debug`):

- `opencode run`: flagget er forespørselens modell og slår agentens frontmatter.
- TUI-en, som er den nav-pilot starter: effektiv modell per agent er valg i økta, så `agent.model`, så flagget, så `config.model`, så recents.

Konfigurasjonsnøkkelen ligger altså under agenten i begge inngangspunkter, mens flagget også ligger under agenten i TUI-en. For en ren sesjonsstandard er de to nesten likeverdige i dag.

Det som ville endret regnestykket:

- Om vi vil sette noe som *ikke* kan uttrykkes som et oppstartsflagg. Per-agent-modeller via `agent.<navn>.model` er det nærmeste eksempelet, og `bindLocalWorker` gjør allerede akkurat det for den lokale arbeideren.
- Om vi vil at standarden skal gjelde utenfor nav-pilot-startede økter, altså at Nav-standarden er maskinens standard.

## Hva som må avklares før noen bygger det

**Eierskap.** Hvilke nøkler eier nav-pilot, og hva skjer med en verdi utvikleren har satt selv? #498 valgte å overskrive `model`, som er én mulig regel, men ikke den eneste.

**Reversering.** Hvis nav-pilot skriver inn en standard og brukeren avinstallerer eller bytter, hvem rydder? `unbindLocalWorker` er presedens for at nav-pilot tar tilbake det den skrev.

**Formatering.** En skriving reserialiserer hele fila og normaliserer utviklerens formatering og nøkkelrekkefølge. En JSONC-fil med kommentarer feiler parsing og degraderer til en advarsel per oppstart.

**Synlighet.** Skriver nav-pilot i en fil utvikleren eier, bør det stå i brukerdokumentasjonen, ikke bare i en kodekommentar.

## Kode som finnes fra forsøket

`mutateOpenCodeConfig` i `cli/nav-pilot/internal/provider/opencode_launch.go` er en lese, mutere, skrive-hjelper med fletting som `EnsureOpenCodeOTelConfig` allerede bruker. Den fikser også en nil-map-panikk: `json.Unmarshal` godtar literalen `null` inn i `map[string]any` og lar kartet være nil, og skriving i et nil-kart paniserer.

Implementasjonen av selve sesjonsstandarden lå på `feat/align-model-semantics` før den ble reversert; historikken i #498 viser den.

Title: Hva skal vi med prompt-filer i nav-pilot?

Vi distribuerer sju prompt-filer, og de når færrest av alle artefaktene våre. Denne saken samler det vi vet, og spørsmålene vi må svare på før vi investerer mer eller trapper ned.

## Det vi har

`prompts/` inneholder sju `*.prompt.md` med hver sin `.metadata.json`: `aksel-component`, `golang-service`, `kafka-topic`, `ktor-endpoint`, `nais-manifest`, `nextjs-api-route`, `spring-boot-endpoint`. Fem samlinger viser til dem (`fullstack`, `frontend`, `nextjs-frontend`, `kotlin-backend`, `platform`).

De fleste av dem er stillasgeneratorer: «lag et Ktor-endepunkt», «lag et Nais-manifest».

## Det som er verifisert i koden i dag

- **Brukerscopet støtter dem ikke.** `ScopeUser()` i `cli/nav-pilot/internal/domain/domain.go:259` lister `agent`, `skill`, `instruction`. Repo-scopet legger til `prompt`. En utvikler med personlig installasjon får dem altså aldri. Installerer du en samling med `--user`, hoppes promptene over og rapporteres; ber du om én enkelt med `--type prompt --user`, er det en feilmelding.
- **opencode får dem likevel.** `opencode_sync.go` skriver hver prompt til `commands/` gjennom `transformPrompt`. Det er verdt å merke seg: opencodes `commands` er den nærmeste analogien til en prompt-fil, og den bevarer det som er poenget med formatet — at et menneske påkaller den bevisst, ved navn.
- `nav-pilot export opencode` håndterer dem på samme måte.

## Hvorfor spørsmålet stilles nå

`SKILL.md` er blitt en konvensjon på tvers av leverandører, og skills-ene våre er dermed portable til Copilot CLI, opencode, Codex, Gemini, Cursor og Junie uten arbeid. Prompt-filer har ingen tilsvarende historie. Samtidig overlapper prompt-filer med tre andre ting Copilot nå har: skills, egendefinerte agenter og chat-moduser.

## Forskjellen som ikke er innpakning

En **skill påkalles av modellens skjønn**. En **prompt påkalles bevisst av brukeren**, ved navn.

For en stillasgenerator er den bevisste påkallingen selve poenget. Gjør vi dem om til skills, håper vi at modellen plukker dem opp — og det er nøyaktig klassen av antakelse uu3 målte til 0 av 5 før vi gjorde regelen strukturell (#517, #557). Vi bør ikke gjenta den feilen i motsatt retning.

## Spørsmål som må besvares

1. **Er formatet i ferd med å bli avløst?** Hva anbefaler GitHub selv i dag for «en gjenbrukbar, parameterisert oppgave en utvikler påkaller med vilje» — er det fortsatt en prompt-fil, eller er veiledningen flyttet til skills eller egendefinerte agenter? Kartlegging pågår; resultatet legges inn som kommentar her.
2. **Hvilke klienter leser `.github/prompts/` i det hele tatt?** Per klient, ikke i snitt.
3. **Skal brukerscopet støtte prompts?** Hvis Copilot CLI leser dem fra `~/.copilot`, er begrensningen vår, ikke plattformens, og da er den verdt å fjerne. Hvis ikke, bør dokumentasjonen si hvorfor tydeligere enn i dag.
4. **Skal noen av de sju bli skills i stedet?** Ikke alle sju er samme sak. En generator og en sjekkliste har ulik påkallingsmodell, og valget bør tas per fil, ikke for hele mappa.

## Hva vi ikke gjør før spørsmål 1 er besvart

Ingen konvertering, ingen fjerning. En omskriving til skills er billig å gjøre og dyr å angre, og den endrer hvem som bestemmer når innholdet brukes.

Henger sammen med #572 (hvilke artefakttyper en agentpakke kan frakte) og #569 (hooks som femte type).

Title: Extensions er kjørbar kode uten samme sandbox-vern som hooks

`hooks` og `extensions` er begge kjørbar kode en agentpakke kan sende med. Bare den ene er vernet mot å bli skrevet fra innsiden av en sandbox.

## Hva som er ulikt

cplt beskytter stiene hooks lander i:

- `~/.copilot/hooks` og `~/.copilot/settings.json` står i host-persistence-deny-lista for Copilot-agenten (cplt `src/agent.rs`, #331)
- `.github/hooks` bindes read-only i prosjektkatalogen (cplt `src/sandbox_policy.rs`, `PROTECTED_IN_ROOT`, #347)

Begrunnelsen står i `internal/cli/hooks.go:168`: en hook-fil er kode som kjører senere, usandboxet, på verten. En prosess inne i sandboxen skal ikke kunne legge igjen en.

Extensions er samme slags ting. `<navn>/extension.mjs` lastes og kjøres av klienten. Katalogene de lander i, `~/.copilot/extensions` og `.github/extensions`, står ikke i noen av listene over.

Det betyr at en agentsesjon inne i cplt kan installere en extension, altså legge igjen kode som kjører utenfor sandboxen senere, mens det samme forsøket med en hook stopper med en forklaring.

## Hva som bør avgjøres

Ikke hva rettelsen er, men hvilken av dem som er riktig:

1. **cplt verner extensions også.** Konsistent med begrunnelsen, og krever en endring i cplt, ikke i nav-pilot.
2. **nav-pilot nekter selv.** Samme forklaring som hooks får i dag, uten å vente på cplt. Raskere, men da håndhever nav-pilot noe cplt ikke gjør, og en bruker som installerer med et annet verktøy omgår det.
3. **Forskjellen er tilsiktet.** Da bør den stå skrevet, for i dag ser den ut som en forglemmelse.

Extensions ble en artefakttype i #739. Før det kjente ikke nav-pilot formen i det hele tatt, så spørsmålet kunne ikke stilles.

Funnet i review av #739, der jeg først skrev i dokumentasjonen at cplt nekter skriving til begge katalogene. Det stemte ikke, og påstanden er rettet i samme PR.

Title: Evaluate: should $TMPDIR process-exec deny be the default?

## Context

cplt currently denies `process-exec` and `file-map-executable` from both temp directories (`/private/tmp` and `/private/var/folders`). The intent is to prevent write-then-exec attacks where a compromised agent drops a binary to a writable dir and executes it.

**Relevant sandbox rules** (`src/sandbox.rs`):
```scheme
(allow file-read*  (subpath "/private/tmp"))
(allow file-write* (subpath "/private/tmp"))
(allow file-read*  (subpath "/private/var/folders"))
(allow file-write* (subpath "/private/var/folders"))

(deny process-exec        (subpath "/private/tmp"))
(deny file-map-executable (subpath "/private/tmp"))
(deny process-exec        (subpath "/private/var/folders"))
(deny file-map-executable (subpath "/private/var/folders"))
```

This breaks tools that write executables or scripts to `$TMPDIR` and then exec them directly — notably **mise** inline tasks (`run = '''...'''`), which always create a temp file in `$TMPDIR` and call `execve()` on it.

## The trade-off

### Arguments for keeping the deny (current default)

- **Prevents binary-drop attacks** — a compromised agent cannot write a native binary to /tmp and execute it.
- **Defense in depth** — even if file-write is allowed, the attacker gains no code execution via temp dirs.
- **macOS `$TMPDIR` is per-user (mode 700)** — so this is about protecting against agent misbehavior, not other users. The sandbox is specifically designed for this.

### Arguments against (or for making it opt-in)

- **Breaks legitimate tooling** — mise, some package managers, and build tools that compile temp executables all rely on exec from `$TMPDIR`.
- **Incomplete protection** — the deny does NOT block interpreter-based execution (e.g., `bash /tmp/script.sh`, `node /tmp/app.js`). The exec target is the interpreter binary (in `/usr/bin` or similar), not the script. An attacker can trivially work around this.
- **`$TMPDIR` is already per-user on macOS** — `/var/folders/<hash>/<hash>/T/` is mode 700, so there is no cross-user attack surface.
- **Causes confusing failures** — the sandbox violation is silent from the tool's perspective; mise just sees an exec failure with no clear cause.

## The bypass gap

The current deny only catches **direct `execve()` calls** on files in temp dirs. It does **not** catch:

| Attack vector | Blocked? |
|---|---|
| Drop native binary → exec it | ✅ Yes |
| Drop `.dylib` → dlopen it | ✅ Yes (`file-map-executable`) |
| Drop script → `bash /tmp/script.sh` | ❌ No (exec target is `/bin/bash`) |
| Drop script → `python3 /tmp/script.py` | ❌ No (exec target is python3) |
| Inline via interpreter | ❌ No |

Since the Copilot agent primarily works through interpreters (Node.js, bash, python), the most likely attack paths are already unblocked.

## Options

1. **Keep as default** — accept the tooling breakage; users can allowlist specific paths via config.
2. **Remove the deny** — rely on other sandbox layers (network restrictions, file-write denies, dotfile protection) to contain the agent.
3. **Make it configurable** — add a config flag (e.g., `allow_tmpdir_exec = true`) that relaxes the deny, defaulting to deny-on.
4. **Narrow the deny** — only deny `file-map-executable` (blocks dylib injection) but allow `process-exec` from temp dirs. This preserves the dlopen protection while allowing tools like mise to work.

## Question

Which option best balances security posture vs. developer experience for the default configuration?

Title: Decide the repo-config trust boundary: macOS/Linux divergence and the --accept-repo-config bypass

Two questions surfaced while fixing #183 (PR #201). Neither is a bug to fix — both need a decision about what cplt's repo-config trust model should be — and they share a root cause, which is why they are filed together.

## 1. The same repo grants different permissions depending on the OS

`src/repo_config.rs:136-153`: on Linux the working-tree fallback is skipped, because Landlock cannot deny individual file writes inside the project directory — a sandboxed agent could rewrite `.cplt.toml` mid-session. On macOS the working-tree file is loaded and applied, with a `⚠ not committed` warning.

Deliberate since #34 (`f6969ab`). The consequence is that an untracked `.cplt.toml` is **live on macOS and inert on Linux**. Same repo, same command, different sandbox.

That matters beyond tidiness:

- A developer on macOS can be working under permissions that CI or a Linux colleague does not have, and neither side gets told.
- The diagnostics added in #201 had to be made `cfg!(target_os = "linux")`-aware precisely because a single honest sentence describing both platforms does not exist. That is a smell: the user-facing explanation is forked because the behaviour is.
- The tamper-resistance argument (read from git HEAD so an agent cannot grant itself permissions mid-session) is the stated security property, and on macOS it does not hold for the working-tree path.

Neither direction is obviously right:

- **Remove the macOS fallback.** Consistent, and the security property holds everywhere. Breaks every existing user who relies on an uncommitted `.cplt.toml` while iterating on their config, and there is no in-band migration.
- **Add a Linux fallback.** Consistent the other way, but weakens tamper-resistance on the platform where Landlock cannot compensate — which is exactly why it was skipped.
- **Keep the split, document it loudly.** Cheapest, and #201's messages already explain each platform correctly. But the divergence stays, and it stays surprising.

## 2. `--accept-repo-config` bypasses the commit guard entirely

`src/main.rs:1367` approves every proposed key with no state check at all. It is explicit per-run and does not persist to the trust store, so it is not the same severity as a persisted approval — but it means an uncommitted, gitignored, or non-git `.cplt.toml` is fully honoured for that run.

## Why these belong together

The commit guard lives in `trust_accept`, not at the `load_repo_config` boundary. That is the structural reason sibling cases keep having to be found one at a time:

- #183/#201 found that `git status --porcelain` is silent for a gitignored file, so a gitignored `.cplt.toml` sailed past the guard and was approved on macOS.
- The same PR then found `NotAGitRepo { has_file: true }` was still approvable, in a *different* branch of the same guard.
- `--accept-repo-config` is the third, and there is no reason to believe it is the last.

Moving the guard to the boundary would fix all three shapes at once and make a fourth structurally impossible. But it is a policy change, not a refactor: it would make an uncommitted `.cplt.toml` inert on macOS — i.e. it decides question 1 in the "remove the fallback" direction as a side effect.

That coupling is the actual decision to make. Fixing 2 properly settles 1.

## Not urgent

#201 closed the exploitable paths that persist to the trust store. What remains is a consistency and a bypass question, both known and now written down.

Title: Decide whether allow_push rules carry URL identity or launch-repository identity

Raised in #423 and worth a deliberate decision rather than leaving it as an assumption in a merged PR body.

## The question

#416 made the git guard check that a push actually runs in the launch repository, by baking its git common directory at launch and comparing at gate time. That closed the case where a push from a repository nested inside the project was judged against the launch repository's baked default branch.

`allow_push` rules were not changed. They authorize on the resolved push **URL**, read live from whichever repository the command runs in. So a nested clone whose `origin` points at a URL an `allow_push` rule permits is still authorized by that rule, even though the guard now knows the push is not running in the launch repository.

## Why it is arguably correct

The URL is the repository's identity. #215 established that the guard should judge a command by the repository it targets rather than by the one the session launched in, and #382 bound `allow_push` rules to destination URLs precisely so a rule names a repository rather than a remote name. Under that reading, "this rule permits pushes to `github.com/me/fork`" should hold wherever the push is issued from, and refusing it because the working directory changed would be the older, wronger behaviour.

## Why it might not be

The two halves of the guard now answer "which repository is this?" differently. `protect_default_branch_only` says the launch repository, identified by its git common directory, captured at launch. `allow_push` says whatever repository the current directory belongs to, identified by a URL read at gate time from config the agent can write on Linux. An operator reading `allow_push = [{remote = "fork", branches = ["agent/*"]}]` is describing what the agent may do in *this* session's repository; they are unlikely to be thinking about a clone the agent might make underneath it.

## What would settle it

Decide which identity `allow_push` is meant to carry:

- **URL identity (no change):** document that an `allow_push` rule authorizes its destination from any repository in the session, and say so where the rules are documented, so it is a stated property rather than an accident of implementation.
- **Launch identity (change):** require that a push authorized by an `allow_push` rule also run in the launch repository, reusing the common-directory check #416 added. Narrower, consistent with the other half of the guard, and it would need a test for the "same rule, nested repo" case either way.

Either is defensible. What is not is leaving the two halves disagreeing silently, since the next person to reason about it will assume they agree.

Title: A .cplt.toml that cannot be parsed stops the launch in a named repository and only warns in the launch one

Introduced deliberately in #468 and worth settling rather than leaving as an inconsistency for the next reader to trip over.

## The current behaviour

- **Launch repository.** `load_repo_config` returns `Err`, and the launch prints `Failed to load .cplt.toml: <reason>` and carries on. The session runs without whatever `[deny]` that file contained.
- **A `--repo-dir` root.** The same failure is fatal: the launch stops, naming the repository and saying its `[deny]` section cannot be applied.

## The argument for making both fatal

It is the same argument, and it is the one #468 acted on for named roots. A `.cplt.toml` that *exists* and cannot be parsed means a restriction its owner wrote is missing. The file is committed, so the operator has every reason to believe it is in force. A warning is exactly the wrong shape for a missing restriction: it scrolls past on the way to a session that runs anyway, and nothing later in the session says the deny is absent.

This is also the shape of several fixes already made here — #214's "absence of information rendered as a clean bill of health", and the `unaudited_roots` warning that exists because measuring nothing must not read as measuring clean.

## The argument for leaving the launch repository as it is

It is long-standing behaviour, and changing it is breaking: anyone with a malformed committed `.cplt.toml` currently gets a warning and a working session, and would get a hard stop instead. The parse error may also be in a section that grants nothing — a mangled `[propose]` block with an intact `[deny]` is indistinguishable from the other way round, because the parse fails whole-file.

There is a real asymmetry in the opt-in, too: a named root is something the user chose to add to this session, and holding an explicitly-added repository to a stricter standard is defensible on its own.

## What would settle it

Whether any repository in the org currently has a `.cplt.toml` that fails to parse. If none does, the breaking change costs nothing and the consistent rule wins. If some do, the fix is to make it fatal *behind the staged rollout* (#264) rather than immediately.

Related: #206, which is about a different half of the same file's trust model.

Title: Avklar gjentatte systembrukeravvisninger og skill PDP-utfall i diagnostikken

## Observasjon

I produksjon hadde `esyfo-narmesteleder` 1 997 WARN-logghendelser med den kodeeide avvisningen «System user does not have access to nav_syfo_oppgi-narmesteleder resource» fra 9. september 2026 kl. 10:36 til 10. september kl. 10:36 (Europe/Oslo).

Antallet gjelder logghendelser, ikke unike systembrukere eller arbeidsgivere. Det beviser verken at tilgangskontrollen er feil eller at delegering nødvendigvis mangler.

## Hva koden viser

- `PrincipalAccessValidator` kontrollerer ressursen gjennom Altinn/PDP. Ved manglende tilgang prøves også organisasjonshierarkiet og systembrukerens organisasjon før det kastes `ForbiddenException` med `MISSING_ALITINN_RESOURCE_ACCESS`.
- `PdpResponse.hasAccess()` returnerer bare true for `Permit`. `Deny`, `NotApplicable` og `Indeterminate` blir alle false. Den samme avvisningsmeldingen kan derfor skjule ulike PDP-utfall.
- HTTP-feil fra PDP-klienten har en separat exceptionsti. Loggene alene skiller likevel ikke de vellykket returnerte beslutningsvariantene.

## Oppgave

- Avklar om avvisningene er forventet trafikk uten rettighet, feil klient-/delegeringsoppsett, unødvendige gjentatte forsøk eller uavklarte PDP-beslutninger.
- Skill beslutningstypene i diagnostikken med lukkede, kodeeide verdier. Ikke eksponer tokens, systembruker-ID, organisasjonsnummer, personopplysninger eller rå PDP-payload i dashboard/issue.
- Avklar om `Indeterminate` trenger annen operativ håndtering enn `Deny`, uten å gi tilgang når beslutningen ikke er Permit.
- Gi avvisningen en strukturert `event_type=api_request_rejected` med lukket `rejection_reason` og relevant kodeeid operasjon. Test både responsen og loggkontrakten.
- Sammenhold mønsteret med aktuell integrasjonseier i godkjent miljø dersom identifikasjon/delegering må undersøkes.

## Dashboardoppfølging

Feiloversiktens gamle filter krevde `api_request_rejected`, og viste derfor ikke disse avvisningene. En avgrenset overgangsleser kan gjenkjenne akkurat denne meldingen for akkurat denne tjenesten, uten å gjøre alle WARN til feil. Erstatt overgangsleseren når produsentkontrakten er ute og relevant historikk ikke lenger trenger den; unngå dobbel telling.

## Ferdig når

- Avvisningsmønsteret har en dokumentert funksjonell forklaring og eventuell eieroppfølging.
- Forventet avvisning kan skilles fra uavklart/teknisk PDP-utfall uten sensitiv metadata.
- Dashboardets avgrensede avvisningsvisning og appens strukturerte logger er avstemt.

Tilgangskontroll og delegeringer skal ikke svekkes eller endres bare for å redusere loggtall. Endringer i tilganger krever egen avklaring.

Title: Decide ownership of the meeting-needs NL syfosmregister gate

## Parent

#15

## Context

The legacy `esyfovarsel` flow has a narrow check that is easy to misdescribe as a general channel gate:

- `AccessControlService` uses KRR `kanVarsles` only.
- Separately, `MotebehovVarselService.sendVarselTilNarmesteLeder` uses `SykmeldingService` and requires a `SENDT` sykmelding for the relevant virksomhet.

Budstikka currently gates on death (PDL) and KRR, but has no equivalent for this meeting-needs NL path. Under ADR 0001 domain blindness, the likely ownership is the producer (`syfomotebehov`), but that product decision has not been made explicitly.

## Decision to make

Decide whether:

1. the producer must enforce the `SENDT`-per-virksomhet condition before publishing;
2. budstikka must implement an equivalent check; or
3. the behavioral difference is intentionally accepted for cutover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The product owner for the meeting-needs flow is identified and participates in the decision.
- [ ] The desired behavior for missing/non-`SENDT` sykmelding is explicit.
- [ ] Ownership is explicit: producer, budstikka, or accepted removal.
- [ ] Cutover criteria and tests cover the chosen behavior.
- [ ] ADR 0009 and `docs/migrering.md` are updated with the decision and rationale.
- [ ] Any implementation work is split into linked, independently testable issues.

## Related

- #151
- ADR 0001: `docs/adr/0001-domeneblind-varselruter.md`
- ADR 0009: `docs/adr/0009-krr-reservasjon-brevfallback.md`
